intro: The Biologische Versuchsanstalt was founded in 1902 by the zoologist Hans Przibram with the botanists Leopold von Portheim and Wilhelm Figdor, who bought the old Vivarium aquarium-hall in the Prater and turned it into the world's first private institute for experimental biology. These are the people behind the 175 papers — founders, assistants, visiting researchers and students. Many were Jewish; after the 1938 Anschluss the institute was seized and its scientists driven out. Some emigrated and shaped science abroad; several — Przibram, Brecher, Zuelzer among them — were murdered in the Holocaust. Each card lists what they wrote here; follow a paper to its English translation or its legacy.

people.name: Hans Przibram
people.bio: Co-founder and scientific director of the Biologische Versuchsanstalt, which he established in 1902 with the botanists Leopold von Portheim and Wilhelm Figdor and led until 1938. A Vienna-born zoologist of independent means, he built the institute into a model of experimental, quantitative biology and worked across regeneration, growth, homeosis, symmetry and the 'crystal analogies' of organic form. Dismissed and dispossessed after the 1938 Anschluss because he was Jewish, he fled to Amsterdam in 1939; deported to the Theresienstadt ghetto in 1943, he died there on 20 May 1944, and his wife Elisabeth took her own life the following day.

people.name: Paul Kammerer
people.bio: The institute's most famous and most controversial figure. Kammerer used fire salamanders, midwife toads and the olm to argue that environmentally induced characters could be inherited — the central claim of neo-Lamarckism. In 1926 the American herpetologist G. K. Noble found that the nuptial pads of his key midwife-toad specimen had been injected with Indian ink; six weeks later Kammerer shot himself in the forest near Puchberg am Schneeberg. Arthur Koestler reopened the affair in 'The Case of the Midwife Toad' (1971), and it is revisited today through the lens of epigenetics.

people.name: Leonore Brecher
people.bio: Brecher took her Vienna doctorate in 1916 on the pupal colouration of the cabbage white and spent two decades at the institute showing how light and background govern butterfly pigment — work now cited in butterfly colour-plasticity research. She was among the first women to seek habilitation at the University of Vienna. Dismissed within days of the 1938 Anschluss because she was Jewish, her attempts to emigrate failed; she was deported on 14 September 1942 to Maly Trostinec and murdered on arrival, four days later.

people.name: Paul Weiss
people.bio: At the Vivarium in the 1920s Weiss carried out the limb-transplantation and regeneration experiments that grounded his concept of the morphogenetic 'field' — the idea that a region, not a pre-existing template, imposes pattern on the regenerate. He left for the United States around 1930, working with Ross Harrison at Yale and later at Chicago and the Rockefeller Institute, and became one of the twentieth century's leading developmental biologists and a founder of systems thinking in biology. His Vivarium papers are still cited in modern axolotl limb-regeneration research.

people.name: Franz Megušar
people.bio: A Slovenian zoologist from Kamna Gorica, Megušar joined the institute in 1904 and became one of its most productive students of regeneration, working across beetles, snails, crustaceans and amphibians. He was killed in the First World War on 3 August 1916 as an Austrian officer-cadet; Przibram wrote his obituary, the one non-research item among these 175 papers.

people.name: Theodor Koppányi
people.bio: A Hungarian-born researcher who, working under Przibram in the early 1920s, performed the institute's sensational eye-transplantation experiments — replanting and transplanting eyes in salamanders, fish and rats. He emigrated to the United States and became a founding figure of modern pharmacology at Georgetown University, author of more than 500 papers.

people.name: Isaak Werber
people.bio: Surveyed regeneration across insects and reptiles — the mealworm beetle's wings and antennae, the lizard's jaws — extending the institute's comparative atlas of who can regrow what.

people.name: Eduard Uhlenhuth
people.bio: Worked on transplantation of the amphibian eye and the 'synchronous metamorphosis' of transplanted salamander organs. His eye-transplant experiments were later cited by Roger Sperry in founding the chemoaffinity hypothesis of neural specificity; Uhlenhuth emigrated to the United States.

people.name: Eugen Steinach
people.bio:
From 1912 Steinach directed the institute's department of physiology. A pioneer of endocrinology, he showed that the interstitial cells of the gonads secrete the sex hormones, and that transplanting the opposite gonad could reverse an animal's secondary sexual characteristics — work that stands as an origin point of hormonal sex-differentiation science and gives him the most-cited paper in this corpus. His 'Steinach operation,' a vasoligature claimed to rejuvenate ageing men, made him world-famous in the 1920s (W. B. Yeats was among those 'Steinached'), and he was repeatedly nominated for a Nobel Prize.

He also carried the theory into human sexuality, holding that homosexuality arose from a mixed 'puberty gland' and could be corrected by replacing the testicles. From 1916 the Viennese surgeon Robert Lichtenstern performed such operations, in a city where same-sex acts were a criminal offence — they remained one in Austria until 1971. Papers in this corpus report those operations and rest on tissue taken during them. The theory is false, the operations did not work, and the idea that sexual orientation sits in the gonad and can be surgically corrected did lasting harm. His place in this history is genuinely contested: some figures in the homosexual emancipation movement of the time welcomed his claim that orientation was innate and organic, when the alternative on offer was that it was a vice.

Jewish, he was lecturing in Switzerland at the time of the 1938 Anschluss and was granted residence there; his wife took her life in Zurich that September, and Steinach died in exile in 1944.

people.name: Slavko Šećerov
people.bio: A Serbian zoologist who studied colour change in the stone loach and contributed to the institute's 'environment of the germ-plasm' program; he later became a public figure in Yugoslavia.

people.name: Bertold P. Wiesner
people.bio: Contributed 3 papers to the corpus: “The replantation of the lens in developed animals” (1923); “The functional capacity of ovaries in rats after autophoric (suture-free) transplantation” (1923); “Raising the body temperature of young brown rats (Mus decumanus) above the normal value and its influence on tail length” (1924).

people.name: Jan Dembowski
people.bio: A Polish biologist who collaborated on the institute's coloration and salamander-pattern studies. He went on to become a leading figure in Polish science and a president of the Polish Academy of Sciences.

people.name: Josef H. Klintz
people.bio: Contributed 3 papers to the corpus: “Regeneration of the antenna in the common woodlouse (Porcellio scaber Latr.)” (1907); “Experiments on the poor regenerative capacity of the Cyclopidae” (1907); “Experimental tail regeneration in dormice (Myoxidae) and some other mammals” (1914).

people.name: Viktor Janda
people.bio: Studied regeneration of the genital organs and the reversal of sex characters in the worm Criodrilus — work still cited in annelid-regeneration research today.

people.name: Walter Finkler
people.bio: Performed the institute's controversial head-transplantation experiments on insects, reporting that swapped heads could still function — results that drew wide attention and considerable skepticism.

people.name: Adolf Walther
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “The environment of the germ-plasm (Part V: The penetration of magnesium into the blood of the freshwater crab, Telphusa fluviatilis)” (1913); “No increase in size of freshly hatched Sphodromantis with the age of the mother” (1914).

people.name: Adolf Černý
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “Experiments on regeneration in freshwater snails (first communication)” (1905); “Experiments on regeneration in freshwater snails and slugs” (1907).

people.name: Raoul Biberhofer
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “On the regeneration of the third maxilliped in the river crayfish (Astacus fluviatilis)” (1905); “On regeneration in Amphioxus lanceolatus” (1906).

people.name: Ferdinand Winkler
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “Studies on Pigment Formation” (1910); “Agreement of positive and negative Dopa reactions on frozen sections with those on extracts (Causes of animal colouration XI)” (1925).

people.name: Oskar Kurz
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “The Leg-Forming Potencies of Developed Newts (Triton)” (1912); “Experiments on Polarity-Reversal in the Newt Leg” (1922).

people.name: Leo Abolin
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “Influencing the Colour Change of Fishes by Chemicals (I: Infundin and Adrenalin on the Melano- and Xanthophores of the Minnow)” (1925); “The regeneration of legs mutilated at the fibular margin in Triton cristatus Laur.” (1930).

people.name: Margarete Zuelzer
people.bio: A pioneering woman protozoologist (Heidelberg doctorate, 1904), Zuelzer worked at the institute on the contractile vacuole and the effects of seawater on protozoa before leading the Protozoa Laboratory in Berlin-Dahlem. Jewish, she was dismissed under the Nazi racial laws in 1933 and fled to Amsterdam; she died of starvation in the Westerbork transit camp in 1943.

people.name: Iginio Sciacchitano
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “When the DOPA forms in the cocoons of Lophyrus pini L.” (1925); “The regeneration of legs mutilated at the tibial margin or medially in Triton cristatus Laur., and a heteromorphosis of the long bone after excision of the fibular margin” (1930).

people.name: Kamil Bogacki
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Experimental fin regeneration in European freshwater fishes” (1906). What it reported: Tail fins regrew in every species tested, dorsal fins partly, pectoral fins not; regrown fins restored their markings; the author judged capacity greatest along the body’s long axis.

people.name: Giovanni Bresca
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Experimental Investigations on the Secondary Sex Characters of the Newts” (1910). What it reported: Castrating adult males made crest, white tail band and head marbling regress within a year; castrated females were unchanged; crest regeneration weakened after castration; gonad grafts failed.

people.name: Henny Burchardt
people.bio: Henny (Henriette) Burchardt worked in the institute's zoological department in its final productive years; her 1930 paper on limbs pushed through the urodele body, in which the cut ends regrew mirror-image distal parts, is among the last of the institute's Archiv series. After the 1938 Anschluss she was among the BVA staff persecuted as Jewish. She was murdered at Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1944, one of five former institute researchers killed by the Nazi regime (with Leonore Brecher, Helene Jacobi, Martha Geiringer and Heinrich Kun). Her name is misspelt 'Burchhardt' in most later bibliographies; the byline of her own paper reads Henny Burchardt.
people._bio_source: Müller (ed.), Vivarium, MIT Press 2017, ch. 1 timeline and ch. 4 (citing Taschwer et al. 2016; Gedenkbuch 2015); paper byline.

people.name: D. R. R. Burt
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “The head and foot of Pelmatohydra oligactis, Pall., as unipotent systems” (1925). What it reported: Head-region rings formed heads and foot-region rings feet at whichever end was free; mid-body tissue could form either, head potential falling aborally; the stock did not influence the graft.

people.name: E. D. Congdon
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “The surroundings of the germ plasm (Part III: The internal temperature of warm-blooded animals (Mus decumanus, M. musculus, Myoxus glis) in artificial climates)” (1912). What it reported: Adult rats reared at 33 °C were 1 °C warmer than at 16 °C; transferred adult rats and mice shifted 1.5–3 °C; rearing temperature did not affect near-pubertal animals.

people.name: Richard Czwiklitzer
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “On the regeneration of the anterior end of Ophryotrocha puerilis Clap.-Metsch.” (1905). What it reported: No regeneration after loss of two or more segments (jaw apparatus expelled, eyes not regrown); after first-segment loss, segment two sometimes grew antennae; antennae with first-segment parts regrew within days.

people.name: Alfred Ehrenpreis
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Spleen transplantation in adult urodeles” (1924). What it reported: Spleens exchanged between newts without vascular sutures healed in, vascularised and kept normal histology with mitoses for up to 122 days in 9 of 25; removed spleens did not regenerate.

people.name: Eugenie Flat-Hauser
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Regeneration of the long bones after partial internal removal in the newt limb (Triton cristatus Laur.)” (1930). What it reported: Proximal halves regrew the missing distal half typically (all 22 regenerates); distal halves regrew mirror images of themselves (23) or atypical forms (13), never the proximal half.

people.name: Alfred Fröhlich
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Colour-Change Reactions in Palaemon” (1910). What it reported: Blinded prawns turn red-brown, then within weeks white (P. treillianus) or pale yellow (P. rectirostris); strong light and white ground contract chromatophores; explained as a nervous reflex from the eyes.

people.name: Theophil Bohdan Gluschkiewitsch
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Regeneration of the anterior and posterior ends of Clepsine tessulata” (1907). What it reported: After 23 days there were 3 complete and 5 incomplete anterior regenerates (of 20) and 2 incomplete posterior ones (of 20); the author concluded leeches are no exception among annelids.

people.name: Goldschmidt
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Regeneration of the bill in the domestic goose (Anser cinereus) and the domestic duck (Anas boschas)” (1909). What it reported: Beak tips cut from three-week-old geese and ducks of both sexes regrew, mostly completely, within 4–6 weeks, with epithelium, bone, connective tissue and tactile corpuscles but apparently no glands.

people.name: Viktor Hammerschlag
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Breeding experiments with Japanese dancing mice and European running mice” (1912). What it reported: Waltzing, albinism and spotting segregated as recessives, with runners to waltzers 4.57:1 and too few spotted mice; a malformed litter sired by a male that lost a leg never recurred.

people.name: Hermann Stieve
people.bio:
An anatomist and histologist of the reproductive organs, Stieve was at Leipzig when he wrote the paper in this corpus, later held the chair at Halle, and from 1935 directed the Anatomical Institute of the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität in Berlin — today the Charité.

In Berlin he arranged to receive the bodies of people executed at Plötzensee prison, most of them women, many condemned for resistance to the Nazi regime. Because an execution date was fixed in advance, he was able to study the effect of prolonged and extreme fear on the female reproductive cycle: a research design that depended on the state killing his subjects to schedule. He published extensively from this material, and undertook to leave no remains behind, so the dead were denied graves. After the war he maintained that he had not known the sentences, and that he had used only the bodies of ordinary criminals. Historians have shown both claims to be untrue.

In 2017 his descendants found more than 300 histological slides from his estate. Thirty-six carried names; fifteen were matched to identified people executed at Plötzensee between 1937 and 1945 — twelve women and three men. They were buried at the Dorotheenstädtischer Friedhof in Berlin on 13 May 2019, which for most of those people is the only grave they have.

His 1920 paper here predates all of this by fifteen years, and is an anatomical study of one intersex person whose body reached Leipzig from a penal institution. It is kept in the corpus because this is a record of what the institute published. The biography is here because a reader who looks him up should not have to find it somewhere else.

people.name: J. A. Bierens de Haan
people.bio: A Dutch zoologist from Amsterdam who came to the Vivarium to work in Przibram's temperature programme. His two 1922 papers measure how closely the body temperature of young brown rats tracks the air around them, and what happens to tail length when that temperature is lowered by chemical means — part of the series Przibram called the Environment of the Germ-Plasm.

people.name: Auguste Jellinek
people.bio: Auguste Jellinek contributed to the institute's eye-replantation series: her 1923 study tested whether a replanted eye restores useful vision, training rats to discriminate feeding vessels by colour and comparing sighted, blinded and transplanted-eye animals. It is a functional rather than histological test — an unusually modern experimental design for the question. She is one of the women named among the institute's scientific staff in the standard history of the Vivarium; between 1920 and 1934, 39 of its 109 listed workers were women.
people._bio_source: Paper byline; Müller (ed.), Vivarium (MIT Press 2017), ch. 1 on the institute's women scientists.

people.name: Josef Halban
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “The increase in size of eggs and newborns with the advancing age of the mother” (1910). What it reported: Egg and newborn size rise with the mother's age — a maternal-age effect on offspring size.

people.name: Jovan Hadži
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Preliminary Experiments on the Biology of Hydra” (1906). What it reported: Green hydra withstood CO2 better than brown; in darkness or green light algae did not enter eggs, one of which still hatched; halved oocytes regained normal size; algae judged non-nutritive.

people.name: Karl Przibram
people.bio: Hans Przibram's younger brother — a physicist known for work on radioactivity, luminescence and colour centres in crystals. His single contribution here brought a physicist's eye to the 'disordered movement' of lower animals, an early brush with what is now the physics of active matter. Also persecuted as a Jew after 1938, he emigrated to Belgium and survived the war, returning afterwards to Vienna.

people.name: Werner Kornfeld
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Dependence of the Metamorphic Gill-Resorption on the Whole Organism in Salamandra maculosa” (1914). What it reported: Grafts show slow degenerative resorption, then abrupt resorption exactly synchronous with the host’s metamorphosis, whatever the donor’s age; the whole organism times gill resorption. No heterochronous case was seen.

people.name: Ferdinand Kryž
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Independence of the coagulation points of specific muscle plasmas from the temperature during life” (1907). What it reported: The coagulation point of muscle plasma is independent of the temperature the animal lived at — a fixed biochemical property.

people.name: Tokuyasu Kudō
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Change in the amount of melanin during colour change in the fishes Esox, Carassius, Phoxinus, Gobius, Nemachilus” (1922). What it reported: The quantity of melanin itself changes during colour change — not only its distribution within chromatophores.

people.name: Kunio Sato
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Can Dopa or tyrosine yield the chromogen in vertebrates?” (1925). What it reported: No DOPA reaction in any vertebrate skin or skin-covering extract, so DOPA is not the usual chromogen; tyrosine tests inconclusive, since protein removal carries tyrosine down; tyrosine remains possible.

people.name: Franz Mayerhofer
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Colour-Change Experiments on the Pike (Esox lucius L.)” (1909). What it reported: Blinded pike darken and stop responding to light but not to electrical or thermal stimuli; in light they grow belly pigment, in darkness pigment regresses; seeing pike pale in darkness.

people.name: Enver Muftić
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Lung regeneration in Salamandra maculosa and some other amphibians” (1907). What it reported: Salamandra, Rana and Bufo lungs regenerate after partial or complete removal when ligated before cutting, via an epithelial regeneration bud; the intact lung hypertrophies; Triton undecided.

people.name: Arthur Neudörfer
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Experiments on the adaptation of freshwater fishes to salt water” (1907). What it reported: Lamprey larvae, sterlet, carp and pike tolerated salt only to a freezing point near −1.0 °C, blood equilibrating with the medium (gills salt-permeable); eel gills judged impermeable.

people.name: Otto Grosser
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Some malformations in the spiny dogfish (Acanthias vulgaris Risso)” (1906). Described a nerveless head fin, gills on the upper jaw, a finless tail and two anterior duplications; Przibram suggested a displaced fin anlage, homoeosis, defect formation and separated cleavage cells.

people.name: Otto Weiss
people.bio: Not to be confused with Paul Weiss: Otto Weiss contributed a single study of regeneration and autotomy in the water spider.

people.name: Reinhard Demoll
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “On the question of the inheritance of characters acquired by the soma” (1920). What it reported: The displaced tooth, which could never have chewed, still bore a grinding surface; Demoll concluded that carp grinding teeth are largely inherited individual acquisitions.

people.name: Rhoda Erdmann
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Endomixis and size variations in pure-bred lines of Paramaecium aurelia” (1920). What it reported: Size means and variability cycle through each roughly four-week intermictic period; after each endomixis a line splits into sublines with different heritable mean sizes, which selection can maintain.

people.name: Sergius Morgulis
people.bio: An American physiologist who used starvation (inanition) as an experimental lever on the growth problem; he later worked in the United States on nutrition and biochemistry.

people.name: Fritz Staudinger
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Heteromorphoses of spiracles and other structures in Carausius (Dixippus) morosus Brunner” (1930). What it reported: Posterior closing plates regrew as mirror-image anterior plates, or not at all; anterior plates and whole spiracles did not regrow; spiracle-like head openings came from a displaced mandibular tendon.

people.name: Henryk Sztern
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Growth measurements on Sphodromantis bioculata Burm. II. Length, breadth and height” (1914). What it reported: No mitoses seen; constant epidermal nucleus density implied cell number doubling per moult; ganglion, thorax and facet dimensions grew by the cube root of 2, with deviations near moult VI.

people.name: A. Landsborough Thomson
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Notes on the regeneration of the fore-limb in various genera of Mantidae” (1922). What it reported: Forelegs of Parathenodera and Stagmomantis nymphs regenerated as miniatures, often with fewer tarsal joints, contrary to Bordage; ganglion punctures failed as movement returned, and no less-differentiated limbs appeared.

people.name: Walter Kolmer
people.bio: Contributed 2 papers to the corpus: “On the finding of a second lens (spontaneous lentoid formation) in the eye of a catfish” (1920); “The replantation of eyes. V. Histological investigations on transplanted eyes” (1923).

people.name: Theodor Weindl
people.bio: Contributed one paper to the corpus, “Pigment Formation on the Basis of Pre-formed Tyrosinases” (1907). What it reported: Melanin-forming tyrosinase occurs in cephalopod skin and eyes but not muscle, in unpigmented squid eggs and in olm skin; reactions needed metal catalysts; living olms pigmented only in light.
